561.tomorrow: The wound that starts a war
561.howItsDone: Many Hindu elders bless a newly married couple to be like Rama and Sita, and Rama's title eka-patni-vrata, vowed to one wife, is part of why; modern writers have also retold this scene from Shurpanakha's side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: on a cold dawn walk, Rama stopped Lakshmana from blaming Kaikeyi. Satyam, priyam: speak what's true, and kindly.
screen: `SATYAM, PRIYAM.`

segments.voice: The quiet ends the way a lot of trouble starts: with someone noticing someone. Rama sits outside the hut, talking with Sita and Lakshmana, when a rakshasi, a woman of the rakshasa people, comes through the trees and sees him. She stops. She wants him, right then, completely. She walks straight up and asks: who are you, dressed like a hermit but carrying a bow, with a wife beside you, in a forest that belongs to rakshasas?
screen: `SOMEONE NOTICES SOMEONE.` → `A RAKSHASI AT THE HUT.` → `WHO ARE YOU, WITH A BOW?`

segments.voice: Rama answers plainly: his name, his father's, Sita's and Lakshmana's, and why they're in the forest. Then he asks who she is. I am Shurpanakha, she says, sister of Ravana, king of the rakshasas, and of Khara and Dushana, who rule this part of the forest. I saw you and I want you. Be my husband. Leave this woman. Then it turns ugly: she says she'll eat Sita, and Lakshmana too. Her name means she of the nails like winnowing fans. Rama's first answer is simple: I'm married, and my wife is here. Then he laughs and suggests she try his brother, and Lakshmana jokes back. Some readers are uneasy with that teasing; others read it as turning aside a dangerous moment without violence. The text doesn't settle it. But hold on to Rama's first answer, because Hindus have. Rama's own father had three chief queens. Rama keeps one. Tradition calls him eka-patni-vrata, the one vowed to a single wife. Years later in the Ramayana, when a great ritual needs his wife beside him and Sita isn't there, he sets a golden image of her in her place rather than marry again. Here's the teaching under it. Hinduism doesn't call desire bad. Kama, desire and love, is one of the four aims of a good life, beside dharma, artha and moksha. But kama is meant to run inside dharma, like a river inside its banks. Shurpanakha is desire with no banks: I want you, so leave her. Rama is desire kept by a vow. That's why many Hindu elders bless a new couple to be like Rama and Sita.

562.title: The wound that starts a war
562.hook: the joking stops when she lunges at Sita, and what follows will start a war
562.carry: karma: every act is a seed
562.howItsDone: The mutilation of Shurpanakha is staged in Ramlila performances and much discussed in modern retellings, and some teachers use the chain from this hut to the war in Lanka to explain karma.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ravana's sister told Rama to leave Sita, and Rama answered first: I'm married. Eka-patni-vrata, Rama's vow of one wife.
screen: `EKA-PATNI-VRATA.`

segments.voice: Sent back and forth between the brothers, laughed at and refused, Shurpanakha turns on the person she blames. It's because of her, she says, looking at Sita. I'll eat her right now, and then you'll be mine. She rushes at Sita, and Valmiki compares it to a great meteor hurtling toward a gentle star. Sita, who has said nothing through all of this, is terrified. There's no more time for jokes.
screen: `SHE BLAMES SITA.` → `A METEOR AT A GENTLE STAR.` → `NO MORE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Rama catches her, holds her back, and speaks sharply to Lakshmana. We shouldn't joke with the cruel, he says. Look how close Sita came. Mark her, so she can't do this again. Lakshmana draws his sword and cuts off her nose and ears. Shurpanakha flees screaming into the forest, to her brother Khara. It's a violent scene, and hard to sit with. Some devotional readers see it simply: she tried to kill Sita, and the brothers stopped her without taking her life. Others, especially modern readers, find it harsh, all the more after the teasing. In some later tellings, like Kamban's Tamil Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, she first comes in a beautiful disguise, and recent writers have retold it from her side. It's fine to hold the discomfort. Now the teaching. Ask most people what karma means and they'll say revenge: she had it coming, so wait and watch. That's not quite the Hindu idea. Karma means action, and the teaching is that every action is a seed. It ripens, sometimes slowly, often through many hands, and it binds the one who does it. Watch the Ramayana show it. A proposal, a joke, a lunge, a sword. The wound goes to Khara. Khara's defeat will go to Lanka. Lanka's pride will go to war. Many teachers read the forest book this way: nobody's act stays small. And it's why the Bhagavad Gita tells Arjuna to do his work without grasping at the fruit. Your part is the seed, planted well; the fruit isn't yours to grab.

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one small thing you did yesterday: a kind word, a favor, a sharp reply. Draw an arrow, and write where it might have traveled: who it reached, who they passed it on to. No judging, just see the seed and its road, and breathe. If you pray, you might offer today's acts to God, as the Gita asks; if not, simply choose one good seed to plant today.

563.title: The omens before Janasthana
563.hook: a wounded sister reaches her brother's court, and an army of fourteen thousand gets ready to march
563.carry: shagun: a good sign for a new start
563.tomorrow: The promise to the sages, kept
563.howItsDone: Valmiki lingers over the omens before the battle at Janasthana, and Hindu families still give shagun, a gift whose name comes from shakuna, a sign, as a good omen at weddings and other new starts.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shurpanakha lunged at Sita, Lakshmana cut off her nose and ears, and she fled to Khara. Karma: every act is a seed.
screen: `EVERY ACT IS A SEED.`

segments.voice: Shurpanakha falls at her brother's feet, covered in blood. Khara rules Janasthana, the rakshasa stronghold in Dandaka, with his general Dushana. He's furious and proud, and both show. Who did this to you? Tell me, and they die today. She tells him: two young men in bark clothes, with bows, and a woman. Khara's first move is almost casual. He sends fourteen rakshasas to kill them, as his sister asks.
screen: `AT KHARA'S FEET.` → `WHO DID THIS?` → `FOURTEEN SENT TO KILL.`

segments.voice: The fourteen reach Panchavati with Shurpanakha pointing the way. Rama asks Lakshmana to stay by Sita and speaks to them first. We live here as hermits, at the sages' request. If you've come to fight, stop where you are. They don't. They hurl their spears, and Rama's arrows cut down all fourteen. Shurpanakha runs back and shames her brother: you call yourself a warrior, and you sent fourteen? Now Khara calls up his whole force: fourteen thousand rakshasas, with Dushana and Trishiras, the three-headed. And Valmiki slows down for the signs. A rain of blood. Jackals howling. The sun dimmed. Khara's left arm throbbing. Khara sees every one and marches on. At the hut, Rama sees signs too, and reads them: a great fight is coming. So he tells Lakshmana to take Sita to a cave hidden by trees. I'll face them alone. Here's the Hindu thread. Valmiki's world is full of meaning, and the epics are full of shakuna, omens: signs that something good or bad is near. The proud man ignores them. The wise one reads them, and acts with care. Hindu families still watch for good signs, and they also make them, on purpose, at every new start. That's where the word shagun comes from: shakuna, a sign. The shagun at a wedding, the money in an envelope, the sweets, the first gifts to the bride, is a good omen given by the people who love her. Many families add one rupee to the sum, a hundred and one, so it doesn't end in zero, and the blessing keeps going.

564.title: The promise to the sages, kept
564.hook: the sages and the gods gather in the sky to watch one man stand in front of an army
564.carry: vachan: rama keeps his word, whatever it costs
564.howItsDone: The battle of Janasthana is told in many Ramlila performances as Rama's promise to the forest sages kept, and Tulsidas's line about the house of Raghu, life may go but not a given word, is still quoted for keeping one's word.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khara's fourteen thousand marched past every omen, and Rama sent Sita to a cave. Shagun: a good sign for a new start.
screen: `A GOOD SIGN FOR A NEW START.`

segments.voice: Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and waits outside the empty hut. Valmiki says the sages, the gods and the celestial beings gather in the sky above Janasthana to watch. Some are worried: one man against fourteen thousand. They pray for him aloud. Then dust rises on the horizon, the drums grow louder, and Khara's army comes into view, a dark mass like storm clouds rolling in.
screen: `ARMOR ON, BOW STRUNG.` → `THE GODS WATCH FROM THE SKY.` → `AN ARMY LIKE STORM CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells the battle over several chapters. Rama's arrows fly so fast that the rakshasas see only his bow, bent into a circle. Dushana leads an assault and falls. Trishiras, the three-headed, comes next, and falls too. Then only Khara is left. He cuts Rama's bow and shatters his armor; Rama takes up another bow and goes on. Khara tears up a tree and hurls it. Rama names what Khara has done: the sages terrorized, the hermits killed. At last Khara falls. The text says it was over in a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour. The gods rain flowers, and Sita comes out of the cave and holds him. Now remember the promise. Not long ago, the forest sages showed Rama the bones of murdered hermits and asked for protection, and he gave his word. Sita even asked whether that word was wise. Today it's kept, at full cost, by one person. This is one of the things Hindus love most about Rama: his word holds. Tulsidas gives it a line that's still quoted: in the house of Raghu, life may go, but a given word may not. The whole Ramayana turns on promises: Dasharatha's to Kaikeyi, Rama's to his father, Rama's to the sages. And it's why the great Hindu rites are built on vows. At a wedding, the couple takes seven steps together around the fire, each step with its own blessing and promise, and the fire is the witness. But one rakshasa, Valmiki says, slipped away. His name is Akampana, and he's heading for Lanka.
screen: `THE BOW BENT INTO A CIRCLE.` · `KHARA FALLS.` · `THE PROMISE TO THE SAGES, KEPT.` · `LIFE MAY GO, NOT A GIVEN WORD.` · then, large: `ONE ESCAPES TO LANKA.`

segments.voice: Hindus begin a puja or a vow with a sankalpa: a short spoken intention, said once, with water held in the palm. Think of a promise you made that turned out harder than you expected. Pick the smallest piece of it you can still keep today, and say it as your sankalpa. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, say it quietly to yourself. Then breathe, and keep it.
Muhurta. A traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes. Rama's battle takes a muhurta and a half. Families still ask a priest for an auspicious muhurta to begin a wedding.

segments.voice: Carry this: vachan, Rama keeps his word, whatever it costs. Tomorrow, the news crosses the sea to Ravana. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: in a muhurta and a half, Rama alone defeated Khara's army and kept his word to the sages, but Akampana escaped. Vachan: Rama keeps his word, whatever it costs.
screen: `VACHAN: A WORD KEPT.`

segments.voice: Until now, the Ramayana has spoken of Ravana without showing him. Now the story crosses the sea, into his city. Akampana arrives in Lanka shaking and tells the king of the rakshasas everything: Janasthana is empty, Khara and Dushana are dead, fourteen thousand lie on the field, and one man did it. Ravana's first response is rage. Who is this man? I'll burn him. And Akampana says: you can't beat him. But I know how you can hurt him.
screen: `ACROSS THE SEA, IN LANKA.` → `ONE MAN DID THIS.` → `I KNOW HOW TO HURT HIM.`

segments.voice: Akampana's idea is cold. Rama has a wife, Sita, and no woman is her equal in beauty, he says. Carry her off, and Rama will die of grief without a single arrow. Ravana takes his chariot across the sea to Maricha, the rakshasa Rama spared years ago at Vishvamitra's sacrifice, who has lived as a kind of hermit since. Maricha says no. Whoever told you this is your enemy pretending to be your friend. Rama is a sleeping lion; don't poke him. Go home. And Ravana listens, and goes home. Then Shurpanakha arrives at his court, wounded, and she doesn't plead. She scolds him in front of everyone: what kind of king are you, lost in pleasure while one man destroys your army? Then she describes Sita, at length. The warning that worked once is about to be overruled. Here's how Hindus read Ravana. He isn't a fool. In the tradition he's learned, mighty, a great devotee of Shiva. What brings him down is ahankara, the ego, the I that has to be the biggest. Good advice reached his mind once. But with his pride stung in public, the ego takes the wheel. That's why every Dussehra, in towns across India and beyond, a giant Ravana goes up in flames at the end of the Ramlila, and many teachers say what burns is ahankara, his and ours. Some read his ten heads as the many faces of pride and craving.
screen: `TAKE HIS WIFE, AKAMPANA SAYS.` · `MARICHA: DON'T POKE THE LION.` · `SHURPANAKHA SHAMES THE KING.` · `AHANKARA: THE EGO.` · then, large: `WHAT DUSSEHRA BURNS.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus bow, or touch an elder's feet, and teachers say the bow is the ego lowering its head. Fold your hands at your heart and bow your head a little. If you pray, bow to God; if not, bow to the day. Recall a time your pride was stung and you wanted to prove something. Breathe out slowly, and let the head stay low a moment longer.
Ravana, 'the one who makes others cry out': the learned king of Lanka, turned back by Maricha, then shamed into the plan by Shurpanakha.
screen: `RAVANA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: ahankara, the pride that Dussehra burns. Maricha's no held, until Shurpanakha spoke. That's day five hundred sixty-five.

566.title: Rama is dharma with a body
566.hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare
566.howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court. Ahankara, the pride that Dussehra burns.
screen: `AHANKARA.`

segments.voice: Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: shores lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and merchants' ships. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage a second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime; he went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit: ramo vigrahavan dharmah. Rama is dharma in bodily form. To steal his wife is to walk into a fire. Look at who's speaking: not a sage, not a friend, but a rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, once hurled across the sea by him. Even his enemy saw it. Hold on to that line, because it's how Hindus learn dharma. Dharma is a big word: right living, duty, truth, the order that holds the world together. It's hard to learn from a definition. So the tradition gives you a person. When a child asks what dharma looks like, many Hindu families point to Rama: keeping his father's word, faithful to Sita, protecting the sages, warning his enemies before he fights. You don't memorize dharma. You watch it, and walk after it.
screen: `BECOME A GOLDEN DEER.` · `PLEASANT WORDS ARE EASY TO FIND.` · `RAMA IS DHARMA IN BODILY FORM.` · `EVEN HIS ENEMY SAW IT.` · then, large: `DHARMA HAS A BODY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who told you something you didn't want to hear that turned out to be true and good for you, the rare kind Maricha talks about. Picture their face as they said it, and notice what it cost them. Let a little gratitude rise. If you can, send them a short thank-you text after the sit.

segments.voice: Hold on to it: dharma has a body, and it's Rama. The rare friend says the hard thing, and the rare listener hears it. See you tomorrow.

567.title: Rama in every tree
567.hook: an old rakshasa admits that he sees Rama behind every tree in the forest
567.carry: smarana: remembering god, even through fear
567.howItsDone: Some Ramayana teachers set Maricha's confession, seeing Rama in every tree, beside the Bhagavata's teaching that a mind fixed on God, even through fear, comes to him; devotees practice smarana on purpose, through the name and Ram naam lekhan, writing Rama's name.

screen: `DAY FIVE-HUNDRED-SIXTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha told his king the hard truth. Pleasant words are easy to find, and dharma has a body: Rama.
screen: `DHARMA HAS A BODY.`

segments.voice: Maricha has given his king the argument. Now he gives him something more personal: his fear. Let me tell you how I know Rama, he says. I was strong once, and proud. I went to break up Vishvamitra's sacrifice, and a boy, barely grown, shot me with one arrow and threw me a hundred yojanas into the sea. I lived. And I didn't learn, not then. It took a second meeting.
screen: `NOT AN ARGUMENT: A FEAR.` → `A BOY WITH ONE ARROW.` → `INTO THE SEA, ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Later, Maricha says, I came into Dandaka with two others, all three of us in the shape of deer, eating sages. Rama saw us and shot three arrows. My two companions died. I ran. Since then I've given all that up. But I can't get away from him. I see Rama in every tree, dressed in bark, holding his bow. I see him in my dreams. Even words that start with his sound, ratna, jewel, ratha, chariot, frighten me. Then Ravana answers. I didn't come for advice. Do as I say, or I'll kill you now. Maricha sees the trap: Rama kills me if I go, you kill me if I don't. Better to die at the hands of an enemy like Rama, he says. And he goes. Now look again at that confession, because Hindu teachers have. Maricha can't stop thinking of Rama. The Bhagavata Purana says something startling about minds like that: the gopis fixed their minds on Krishna through love, King Kamsa through fear, others through hatred, and all of them came to him, because their minds were full of God. Remembering God has a name, smarana, and it's one of the classic forms of bhakti. Maricha does it by accident, out of fear. Devotees do it on purpose, out of love: saying Rama's name through the day, writing Shri Ram line after line in a notebook. In Tulsidas's telling, Maricha even goes gladly, thinking at least he'll see Rama before he dies. And the week behind us: a proposal and a wound, an army and a promise kept, a king's pride, and an old enemy who couldn't stop seeing Rama.
screen: `I SEE RAMA IN EVERY TREE.` · `OBEY, OR I KILL YOU NOW.` · `LOVE, FEAR OR HATRED: THE MIND ON GOD.` · `SMARANA: REMEMBERING GOD.` · then, large: `BETTER TO DIE BY RAMA'S HAND.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your eyes close. If you pray, let a name of God ride on your breath: Ram, or whichever name is yours, once in, once out. When your mind wanders, and it will, bring it back to the name. If you don't pray, use a word that steadies you, like peace. Maricha couldn't stop remembering. Here, you choose to.
